summary: Abhay Bhushan's summary of the February 23, 1973 Network Mail meeting at SRI-ARC and what it implied for FTP. The meeting agreed that mail belonged within FTP, which already had MAIL and MLFL commands, and the paper discusses what a network mail system should provide. It is a discussion paper.

eli5.summary: A report on a meeting about how computers should pass letters to each other, concluding that the file-sending program should carry them.

subtitle: A 1973 discussion paper on putting network mail inside FTP, with six mail functions and new commands.

tldr.problem: FTP already had two mail commands, but a February 1973 meeting agreed that network mail should live within FTP, and FTP lacked facilities for recording mail, sender addresses, citations, acknowledgments and message types.
tldr.mechanism: The paper breaks a mail system into six functions (creating, locating, sending, storing, recording, reading), describes four usage models and the role of the NIC, and proposes new FTP commands such as MLTO, FROM, MTYP, RECO, AUTH, TITL, ACKN, TEXT, FILE and CITA.
tldr.outcome: It is a discussion paper that records the author's understanding of the meeting and proposes an approach; it does not itself change FTP.

today: The status in the unit data is Unknown and no later RFC is recorded as replacing it. It is a 1973 discussion paper, useful as a record of early thinking about network mail inside FTP.

sections.title: Mail Inside FTP
sections.content:
The paper gives the author's understanding of the Network Mail System meeting at SRI-ARC on February 23, 1973. There was general agreement that the network mail function should be within FTP.

FTP already had two mail commands. MAIL sends mail over the TELNET connection, and the server finds the end by searching for the sequence CRLF.CRLF. MLFL (mail file) sends mail over the data connection, which is more efficient because the server need not search for a special sequence, though it needs a user-FTP to handle the command.

A network mail system should let users send messages to others with mailboxes at one or more hosts. Delivery need not be real time, and it is not an interactive or general inter-process communication facility.
sections.eli5: The file-sending program already knew two ways to mail a letter. People wanted to make that the official way and make it better.

sections.title: Six Mail Functions and Four Models
sections.content:
The paper says a network mail system should provide six functions:

  • Creating: the sender composes the message, using local editing conventions.
  • Locating: finding the receiver's address; the NIC would maintain and publish mailbox addresses.
  • Sending: directly, or through an intermediate host such as the NIC.
  • Storing: the receiver is responsible for storing mail.
  • Recording: cataloguing mail, possibly sending only a citation of a large document.
  • Reading: how the receiving site presents mail to the user.

Four usage models follow: connect directly to the destination FTP server and use MAIL; compose locally and send with MAIL or MLFL; use an intermediate site such as the NIC with NIC idents; or send a citation instead of the whole item.
sections.eli5: Sending a letter has six steps: write it, find the address, post it, keep it, file it and read it. The paper looks at each one.

sections.title: TIP Users, Access Control and the NIC
sections.content:
The TIP had no FTP server or mailbox facilities. The paper argues that TIP users should rent mailboxes at their "home-base" host rather than receive mail at a TIP terminal, because of the risk of lost mail and lack of privacy.

On access control, it reports a suggestion that receiving mail should be "free", meaning no USER, PASS and ACCT login, with costs charged to an overhead account. It argues the USER command is not the best way to identify a sender and proposes a separate FROM command. The NIC is described as a special mail facility that was overloaded and awkward to use via NLS; delivering mail to users by FTP is proposed as faster.
sections.eli5: People using simple terminals should get a mailbox at their usual computer. Mail should be easy to send, and the sender should say who they are.

sections.title: Proposed FTP Commands
sections.content:
Three approaches are offered for the missing features: hide them in the pathname syntax of MAIL and MLFL, add new commands, or define a new mail command set while gradually phasing out the old ones. The author prefers the third, since existing mail programs keep working.

The proposed commands are MLTO (recipients, starting the sequence), FROM (sender address), MTYP (type U urgent, O ordinary or L long), RECO (record the mail), AUTH (author), TITL (title), ACKN (acknowledge), TEXT (send over TELNET like MAIL), FILE (send over the data connection like MLFL) and CITA (citation by pathname). New reply codes are also needed. The RDML and RDMF commands of RFC 458 are also worth considering.
sections.eli5: The paper lists new buttons for the mail machine: who it is to, who it is from, how urgent it is, and whether to tell the sender it arrived.

items.label: Mail to
items.desc: One or more mailbox identifiers, comma separated; starts the mail command sequence.

items.label: Sender
items.desc: Address of the sender or senders, for replies and acknowledgments.

items.label: Mail type
items.desc: U urgent, O ordinary (the default) or L long.

items.label: Record
items.desc: Record the mail, optionally with identifying information such as a NIC Journal number.

items.label: Author
items.desc: Identifies the author of the document.

items.label: Title
items.desc: The title, an ASCII string ending with CRLF.CRLF.

items.label: Acknowledge
items.desc: Ask a forwarding site to acknowledge delivery or failure within a specified time.

items.label: Text
items.desc: Start the mail transfer over the TELNET connection, as MAIL does.

items.label: File
items.desc: Start the mail transfer over the data connection, as MLFL does.

items.label: Citation
items.desc: Pathname of a retrievable file, sent instead of the whole item.

references.text: Bressler, R. and Thomas, R., NWG/RFC 458 (RDML and RDMF commands).
